scenes.text: Syllabus four point one, excerpt limiting friction and limiting equilibrium. By the end, you can choose friction’s direction at each limit. And find the range of forces maintaining equilibrium.

scenes.title: One block, two limits

beats.text: Consider a box held still on a rough slope by an uphill force. We can adjust that force while the box remains in place.
At the smallest force that holds it, the box is just about to slip downhill. Friction helps the applied force, acting uphill.
Now consider the largest force that still leaves it at rest. The box is just about to move uphill. Friction reverses and acts downhill.
The box stays stationary in both limiting cases. The arrows show forces, not motion. We will find both limits for this same box.

scenes.title: The complete question

beats.text: A particle of mass four kilograms rests on a fixed rough plane.
The plane is inclined at thirty degrees to the horizontal.
The coefficient of friction is zero point two five.
Take g as ten metres per second squared.
A force P acts uphill, parallel to the line of greatest slope. Contact is maintained; there are no other applied forces.
Find the minimum and maximum values of P that keep the particle in equilibrium. Both unknowns belong to this one question. Let’s resolve the forces.

Take g as ten metres per second squared. A force P acts uphill, parallel to the line of greatest slope. Contact is maintained. There are no other applied forces. Find the minimum and maximum values of P that keep the particle So, in equilibrium, both unknowns belong to this one question. Let's resolve the forces.

scenes.title: Resolve weight and find the reaction

beats.text: Resolve parallel and perpendicular to the plane. Replace weight by its two components; do not add the original weight again.
The applied force and friction are parallel to the slope. Neither has a perpendicular component. Since contact is maintained, the perpendicular resultant is zero.
Reaction minus m g cosine theta equals zero.
Hence reaction equals m g cosine theta.
Substitute mass four, g ten, and angle thirty degrees.
This gives reaction twenty root three newtons.
The component of weight down the slope is m g sine theta.
Four times ten times sine thirty degrees gives twenty newtons down the slope.

scenes.title: Friction has a limit

beats.text: For a stationary particle, the magnitude of actual friction is at most mu R. Equality applies at limiting equilibrium.
Maximum friction equals mu R.
Substitute zero point two five and reaction twenty root three.
The friction limit is five root three newtons.
That limit is the same in both cases because the uphill force has no normal component. We use the full limit only at the endpoints. Between them, friction adjusts.

scenes.title: Minimum P: friction helps uphill

beats.text: For the minimum uphill force, impending motion is downhill. Friction therefore points uphill and reaches its limit. The particle is still at rest.
In equilibrium, the parallel resultant is zero. Applied force plus limiting friction minus the downhill weight component equals zero.
Insert friction five root three and downhill weight component twenty.
Rearrange: minimum P equals twenty minus five root three newtons.
To two decimal places, the minimum force is eleven point three four newtons uphill.
Friction supplies the rest of the uphill support. If P were any smaller, even maximum uphill friction could not balance the downhill weight component.

scenes.title: Maximum P: friction opposes uphill

beats.text: For the maximum uphill force, impending motion is uphill. Friction now points downhill, at its full limit. Again, this is equilibrium, so the particle remains stationary.
The parallel resultant is zero. Applied force minus limiting friction minus the downhill weight component equals zero.
Insert friction five root three and downhill weight component twenty.
Rearrange: maximum P equals twenty plus five root three newtons.
To two decimal places, the maximum force is twenty eight point six six newtons uphill.
Here friction joins the downhill weight component to oppose P. Any larger force would exceed their combined resistance. The two limits include their endpoints.

scenes.title: Inside the range, friction adjusts

beats.text: Equilibrium is possible from the minimum to the maximum, including both. At each endpoint, friction is limiting; inside the range its magnitude is smaller.
What would change if P exactly balanced the downhill weight component? Would friction still have its maximum value?
No. Taking uphill as positive, parallel balance is P minus the downhill weight component plus signed uphill friction equals zero.
With P equal to twenty newtons, twenty minus twenty plus f equals zero.
So actual friction is zero. Below this balancing force it acts uphill; above it, downhill, as long as equilibrium is possible.
Choose friction’s direction at each limit.
